newsitem.title: MADAGASKAR: Madagascar court confirms president's impeachment.
newsitem.headline: Madagascar court confirms president's impeachment.

text.p: Madagascar's constitutional court confirmed on Thursday the impeachment of President Albert Zafy and ordered his prime minister to take over his duties until an election.
In a ruling on a parliamentary vote in July to impeach him, the High Constitutional Court said it "declares the definitive impeachment of the president of the republic Albert Zafy".
The court said the order by the president of the national assembly for Zafy's impeachment was regular and admissable on the grounds that the president had violated the constitution.
The court noted the subsequent "vacancy in the post of president" and designated Prime Minister Norbert Ratsirahonana to take over his duties until a new head of state was elected.
Zafy was expected to address the nation by radio later.
Before the court ruling, the next presidential election was not due until 1998, a year after parliamentary polls.
Zafy had said the constitutional court was not empowered to decide whether to dismiss him and had refused to accept the parliament vote in July by 99-32 in favour of his impeachment.
Only 92 votes, or two-thirds of all members of the national assembly, are needed for an impeachment motion to pass.
Parliament invoked what it said were Zafy's repeated violations of the constitution and accused him of acting against the interests of the Malagasy people.
Zafy would not be barred from the new presidential election.

The crisis, unique in the country's history, was a result of growing opposition to Zafy, who won Madagascar's multi-party elections in 1993, defeating former military ruler Didier Ratsiraka after 17 years in power.
But democracy brought no improvement in the material lives of the 14 million islanders, among the poorest people on earth.
Zafy, a 68-year-old professor of surgery and downbeat man of the people in his trademark straw hat, emerged as the figurehead of opposition to Ratsiraka in strikes and rallies in 1991.
Madagascar's army has pledged to uphold the constitution and rule of law during the crisis between parliament and Zafy.
The managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said during a visit earlier this year that he was shocked by Madagascar's economic decline since his last trip in 1991.

Before the visit, Zafy had relied on and defended "parallel financing" -- private loans ostensibly for development projects but at far higher interest rates than from multilateral donors such as the IMF.
Madagascar last month signed undertakings with the IMF and World Bank on economic reforms expected to pave the way for a three-year Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility and debt rescheduling.
Madagascar has a total foreign debt of some $4 billion.
Zafy won a referendum last September that gave him the power to name the prime minister instead of the national assembly.
In June, he rejected an initial list for a new government submitted by Ratsirahonana, a former head of the constitutional court, on the grounds it did not include five names he wanted in the cabinet.
